newsitem.title: COOK ISLANDS: French Polynesia opposition leader boosted by vote.
newsitem.headline: French Polynesia opposition leader boosted by vote.

text.p: French Polynesian pro-independence leader Oscar Temaru said during a visit to the Cook Islands at the weekend that support for his party had jumped sharply in the recent French parliamentary elections.
Temaru is in Rarotonga for just over a week to seek backing for the inclusion of the French overseas territory on the agenda at September's South Pacific Forum meeting here.
This has not been forthcoming from Cook Islands Prime Minister Sir Geoffrey Henry, however.

Temaru's Tavini Huiraatira (Polynesian Liberation Front) opposition party emerged from the election with about a third of the votes -- a result its leader said showed "growing popularity of the Maohi people's aspiration for self-determination and the support for our grass roots party".
Maohi are the indigenous Eastern Polynesians who make up around 70 percent of the population of the Tahiti-Polynesia island grouping.
Temaru said his party's support rose by 77 percent compared with the 1993 election. Official confirmation of the figures was not initially available.
"The party is considered a major force both locally and internationally with 35 percent of the total voters," he told Reuters.
"The concept of a sovereign country ruled by the Maohi people for the Maohi people of Tahiti-Polynesia is no longer considered a taboo," he added.
Temaru's aim has for some time been to build support among Pacific Forum nations for a concerted call for independence in the five French archipelagos, also known as Tahiti Nui.
He believes that there are parallels with the case of New Caledonia, which was re-inscribed on a United Nations' list of non-self-governing territories in 1986 after troubles there.

While his rallying calls have found some support locally in the Pacific, with Cook Islands opposition leader Norman George giving his backing at the weekend, others point out the case is very different.

Cook Islands' premier Henry, in a letter widely publicised in the region, told Temaru he believed the French-Polynesian case should be handled internally as Tahiti Nui has a democratically elected government, unlike New Caledonia.
The letter said "...that difference will not escape the notice of (South Pacific) Forum leaders.

"It is, therefore, more than likely that the issue of U.N. involvement in the self-determination process in Tahiti Nui would be viewed as very much a last resort and not be pursued so long as progress was seen as taking place in the political evolution..., which has obviously been the case," he went on.

Temaru's party currently holds 11 of the 41 seats in the French Polynesian assembly following last year's territorial elections, but he said that his party's share of the French vote translated to an equivalent increase of nearly three seats.

Although a coalition of pro-French parties between Gaston Flosee's Tahoeraa (Popular Union) and Emile Vernaudon's Ai'a Api (New Country) holds the majority of the territorial assembly seats, Temaru said he believed that arrangement could break up.
